item.title: The Threat of AI Agents: LLMs are Being Deprecated in 6 Months. Why and How to Prepare
item.description:
Model IDs hardcoded into your code are dependencies with expiration dates, much like an unsupported library version. For Anthropic's flagship models, this date typically arrives about a year after release. Google's preview models expire within months, and the window between deprecation announcements and actual shutdowns for providers ranges from 28 to 182 days. We've analyzed what was shut down and when in 2026, what breaks, how teams actually migrate (based on a sample of 17,703 repositories), and how to build an application that can survive model changes without a crisis. Read on.

item.title: Slopsquatting: How We Spent 20 Years Teaching Developers Not to Trust Packages, Then All Trusted LLMs Together
item.description:
For twenty years, the cybersecurity community has been teaching developers not to pull unverified dependencies into their projects. Then we started trusting LLMs to write code, and they happily invent non-existent packages, leaving attackers only to register them first. Let's explore what slopsquatting is, how often models hallucinate packages, and how to protect against it. Read more

item.title: All 179 responses were SURE. Four of them failed tests
item.description:
The idea was simple, almost naive: if you ask the model to honestly state at the end of its response whether it's confident in its code or not, can you use this label to catch bad solutions in advance? Not run tests, not read code with your eyes, but just look at the last line. I ran 20 small Python tasks through three models, three times each, and collected 179 responses. All 179 ended with the line CONFIDENCE: SURE. The UNSURE option was in the prompt, but no one used it. However, four solutions failed hidden tests. One converted 1024 bytes to 1.0 MiB, another crashed on the difference between two ordinary dates. Both had SURE under them. I'll explain how it was set up, show all four errors, and honestly list what cannot be drawn from this experiment (and much cannot). Read more

item.title: [Translation] Where to Find Opportunities in the B2C AI Segment
item.description:
Hello! My name is Sasha Zhuravlev. I am a venture investor and founder of the Mento vc fund. We invest in startups at the Seed/Series A stages in the USA, and on my Telegram channel, I share my market insights and investment decisions. a16z (a VC fund with over $100B under management) has released a report on the state of the B2C AI market. It compiles data on web traffic (and payments) for various AI applications, compares them, and draws conclusions. My team and I have translated a breakdown of all the theses and charts for you. Inside, you'll find answers to questions like: • Which services and applications attract the most users, and which ones do people spend the most on? • What problem must a product solve for a person to be willing to pay for it every month? • What needs to be offered to those who don't pay yet to make AI a part of their daily lives? • Which niches are still open, and where might the next big player emerge? Enjoy reading! The a16z team has been monitoring the AI services market for private users for three years, and the lineup of leaders is becoming increasingly established. Based on traffic alone, it's becoming harder to understand what's really happening in the B2C AI market. Therefore, in this issue, a16z is adding a ranking based on the spending of American users with personal bank cards for the first time, based on YipitData. This ranking shows which AI products people are actually paying for. It will include services that fly under the radar of website traffic and mobile app audience rankings: for example, desktop versions or AI agents in messengers. Read more

item.title: Jev 1.14: Finding Objects, Verifying Documents, and Spotting a Cat Among 96 Photos
item.description:
In the previous article, I tested Jev on text-based tasks: classification, answer confidence, long context, and noisy input. On October 14th, TypeSafe announced Jev 1.14, introducing experimental capabilities for images, a new 'box' question type, and extended context. I wanted to see what could be done with these new features in practice and where errors might occur. A quick series of experiments allowed me to test object detection by description, cat and dog breed classification, image-based questions, finding bank details on documents, and queries with dozens of photos. The total cost for all computations was around $2.6. The most telling result came from the 'find the cat among dogs' task. With 32 and 96 photos, the model never selected the correct photo from the middle of the array. After changing the query structure—same images, same order—it answered correctly in all tested cases. Below, I'll explain what exactly changed and why the initial result was easily misinterpreted. Read on.

item.title: From Sandpaper to AI: How Technologies Solve Problems
item.description:
Abrasive materials are an essential tool for homeowners, used for sanding wood, cleaning metal, and preparing surfaces for painting. In construction, the quality of abrasives directly impacts the finish of walls and floors, and ultimately, the aesthetic appeal and comfort of a home. In manufacturing, the precision of abrasive processing determines the final quality of parts. For manufacturers, the quality of abrasive products is a matter of prestige and customer loyalty, ensuring their brand of abrasives won't let them down. We're talking about the Belgorod startup 'Solid' – an intelligent visual analytics platform for quality control of abrasive products. It was created by students from Belgorod State Technological University named after V. G. Shukhov (BSTU) and was developed at the inter-university accelerator 'Homenet,' implemented as part of the Federal Project 'Technologies.' Read more

item.title: How to run Super Mario Bros on Xiaomi Mi Band 4
item.description:
